title: After a Spell executes, ds-pause re-checks that the Pause Proxy is still owned by ds-pause
content:
A.1.10.2.4.13.4.2 walks through execution inside the cast transaction: `ds-pause` validates and removes the scheduled entry, then "calls `exec` on the Pause Proxy contract, which performs a **`delegatecall`** to the Spell action contract address specified during scheduling." After the actions run, step 5: "**Final Checks**: If the transaction succeeds, the `exec` function in `ds-pause` performs a final ownership check to ensure the Pause Proxy is still owned by `ds-pause`."

The check exists because of the delegatecall. Running by delegatecall means the Spell's code executes in the Pause Proxy's storage context with the proxy's full authority — including, in principle, the authority to change who owns the proxy. That is the single most dangerous thing a Spell could do, because it would detach the protocol's execution engine from governance permanently and irreversibly.

Making the assertion *after* the actions rather than before is what makes it effective. A pre-check proves nothing about what the actions will do; a post-check tests the state they actually left behind. Since the whole thing is one transaction, a failed assertion reverts everything, so a Spell that attempts to orphan the Pause Proxy accomplishes nothing at all.

This is a self-preservation invariant expressed in code rather than in rules: whatever else governance authorizes, it cannot authorize the destruction of its own control path, because that outcome cannot survive the transaction that produces it.

Step 4 handles the mundane counterpart — "If the transaction reverts at any point (e.g., due to an error in `actions()`), the Pause Proxy halts execution" — giving Spells all-or-nothing semantics, so a partially applied Spell is not a possible state.
description: A.1.10.2.4.13.4.2 adds a post-execution ownership assertion, so a Spell running by delegatecall in the proxy's context cannot sever governance's control and survive.
